fields.title: Restore four deleted verify suites and revert eight amended
fields.description: Restore from git history the four landed verify suites deleted by the background-agent removal and revert its amendments to eight others, since landed verify suites must not be edited.
fields.notes: E-2074 deleted four landed verify suites for the features it removed and amended eight more where they asserted on what it took out, with its own suite asserting the four are gone.
fields.context: Mike, on being shown this during E-2081: E-2074 BADLY VIOLATED the principles of Endless.
fields.analysis:
Deleted by E-2074 (commit bf285b54): the e-1568, e-1570, e-1572 and e-1621 verify suites. Amended by the same commit: e-1573, e-1624, e-1645, e-1648, e-1659, e-1905, e-1906, e-1914, e-1967 and e-2067. Its rationale was 'a suite that proves a deleted feature works is worse than no suite'.

The guide's answer to that concern is different and already written: leave the suite alone, let it fail, and move coverage that must survive into the durable suite (just test, go test). A landed suite is a record, not a regression test, so a stale one costs nothing — nothing under tests/tasks/ is imported, executed at build time, or read by the product.

Restoring the four is a straight git revert of those paths. The twelve amendments need reading one at a time: some are pure retrofits to keep a suite green and revert cleanly, but E-2074's own message claims three of them (e-1573, e-1914, e-2067) fixed real pre-existing leftovers its sweep caught — decide per file whether the restored text is the honest historical record or was already wrong when it landed.

Then E-2074's own verify script needs its assert_absent block on the four deleted paths replaced, since after this they exist again.

The violation propagated before it was caught: E-2081, working the same kind of removal three days later, read E-2074 as the convention and deleted E-1682's suite, amended e-2071 and e-2037, and ran both. All of that was reverted. E-1916 (block edits and runs of landed suites from the PreToolUse hook) would have refused every one of those moves at the tool call and is still only submitted; until it lands, the rule is prose an agent can rationalise past — and this is twice now that one did.

## From the description

That inverts the rule: a landed verify suite is a one-shot land-time gate whose post-land pass/fail is undefined, and it must not be edited because it records what was true when its task landed — deleting one being the strongest possible edit.

fields.title: Review what must land or move before the Go port
fields.description: Review which open tasks and which unsettled worktrees must land before the Go port starts, proposing a blocker list, landing order and any re-parents for approval.
fields.context: Two questions must be answered before E-1063 can start, and neither yields to a keyword search.
fields.analysis:
## Already done, do not redo

- E-1063 is type `epic` (it was `todo`).
- E-1486, E-894 and this task are its direct children. The tree is deliberately
  FLAT: nested tasks make it hard to see what needs doing, so add depth only
  with a reason worth stating.

## Measured 2026-08-28

- 136 worktrees on disk under `.endless/worktrees`.
- 84 of them unsettled. `endless task unsettled --all` is the survey command and
  it paginates at 20, so pass `--no-limit`.
- Some carry very large unlanded counts: E-1844 at 223 commits, E-1785 at 198,
  E-1853 at 182, E-1829 and E-1834 at 11 each. A high count usually means the
  branch is far behind main rather than that it contains that much work; check
  before treating it as a large change.
- One row reads `(no task row)` — E-1279. A worktree whose task is gone is its
  own small decision.
- 57 open tasks match a Go-or-Python keyword sweep. Treat that as a candidate
  pool to triage, NOT as an answer. Most will be incidental mentions.

## Question 1 is mostly about ORDER, not ownership

The expected outcome is a set of `blocked_by` edges on E-1063, not a pile of new
children. Three buckets, and most candidates land in the third:

- BLOCKER — the port would clobber this work, or this work must exist first.
  Record as `endless task block E-1063 --by <id>`.
- CHILD — this IS part of moving the surface to Go. Expected to be a short list.
- NEITHER — mentions Python or Go incidentally. Leave it exactly where it is.

A fourth bucket worth calling out if you find it: tasks the port SUBSUMES, which
stop existing once Go owns the surface. Those are obsolete-on-land candidates,
not blockers — flag them, do not close them.

## Question 2 method note

The risk is not "unlanded work exists". It is "unlanded work that touches Python
the port will delete". A worktree editing only Go, docs or tests is cheap to land
after the port; one rewriting `src/endless/task_cmd.py` is not. Sort by what the
branch touches, not by how long it has sat.

Also worth checking: whether a worktree branched before E-1891 can still run
`endless` at all. That landing broke worktrees whose stale `endless-go` predated
the status registry, because `cli.py` imports the registry at module level ahead
of the re-exec that would route around it. A worktree that cannot run the CLI
cannot easily be landed by its own session.

## From the description

A few may genuinely belong UNDER E-1063; treat that as the smaller, secondary finding.

Deliver a proposed blocker list, a proposed landing order, and any proposed re-parents, each entry with a one-line reason, for Mike to approve before anything is moved or landed.

fields.title: Install the tmux integration from endless setup
fields.description: Install the tmux integration from endless setup, writing the tmux config line that triggers it, so it survives tmux server restarts without a manual apply.
fields.context:
'endless setup' has no tmux subcommand and setup.py contains zero tmux references, so the tmux-conf line that 'endless tmux init' documents as its own trigger is never written — making init unreachable for anyone who has not hand-edited their tmux config. The only working path is running 'endless tmux apply' by hand, which is ephemeral and must be repeated after every tmux server restart, and the reference guide documents apply without ever mentioning init or the conf line.

So a PRODUCT user gets no second status row, no popup menus, and no way to make either persist.

fields.title: Fix task unsettled counting rebased commits as unlanded
fields.description: Fix task unsettled and the session-status marker to compare commits by patch-id, so commits landed rebased onto main no longer count as unlanded.
fields.context:
endless task unsettled --all reports 86 unsettled worktrees; git cherry (patch-id) over the same population gives 14.

E-1934 reports 314 unlanded commits and holds 2; E-1844 reports 223 and holds 4.
fields.analysis:
## Evidence (measured 2026-08-30)

`endless task unsettled --all` reported 86 unsettled worktrees. Re-running the
same population through `git cherry main <branch>` — which matches by patch-id
rather than SHA — gives 14 branches holding any commit not already on main.

Worst offenders, reported vs. actual:

| Branch | `unsettled` says | `git cherry` says |
|---|---|---|
| E-1934 | 314 | 2 |
| E-1844 | 223 | 4 |
| E-1785 | 198 | 2 |
| E-1853 | 182 | 6 |
| E-1537 | 122 | 2 |

## Cause

`worktree land` rebases the branch before fast-forwarding main. The rebase
rewrites SHAs, so main receives a copy of each commit under a new hash while
the branch retains the original. Any check based on "is this SHA reachable from
main" reports the branch's copies as unlanded permanently, and the number grows
with every subsequent land on the branch.

## Why it matters

The count is the input to every "what is outstanding?" judgement. At ~6× it
makes a 14-branch backlog look like an 86-branch one, and it buries the handful
of branches that genuinely hold work under a pile that does not. It also makes
the number grow over time for branches that are *more* settled, not less.

## Scope

Replace the SHA-reachability check with a patch-id comparison (`git cherry`, or
`git log --cherry-mark --left-right`) in whatever `unsettled` and the `session
status` ◆ probe share — the two read the same probe by design and must keep
doing so.

Note the separate case the fix should keep visible: a branch can carry patches
that are genuinely absent from main and still be undesirable to land, because
main has moved past them by another route. Four branches here (E-1537, E-1785,
E-1844, E-1934) hold only a README rewrite that E-1832 superseded. Patch-id
correctly calls those unlanded; it is the operator who has to decide they are
not worth landing. That is out of scope here — just do not paper over it.



## Correction from E-2089: patch-id is not sufficient — use `git range-diff`

E-2089 re-measured this population and found the prescribed fix falls short.
Patch-id survives a plain rebase, but `worktree land` rebases onto a moving main
and conflict resolution CHANGES the diff — after which the branch copy and the
landed copy have different patch-ids and read as unlanded forever. The four
README branches named above are exactly that case, and the earlier reading of
them as "genuinely absent from main" was wrong:

- `98bb7b24` landed as `785fe07b`; `4e611073` landed as `a8bfccff`. Same
  subjects, different SHAs AND different patch-ids. E-1832 is `confirmed` and
  its README rewrite is on main.
- `git cherry` still reports both as `+` on E-1803, E-1864, E-1865 and E-1929,
  which is the false positive this task exists to remove.

`git range-diff` pairs two commit series by content SIMILARITY rather than exact
patch-id, so a conflict-resolved commit is still matched to its landed
counterpart. Measured over every branch in this repo:

```
B=$(git merge-base main "$BR")
git range-diff "$B..$BR" "$B..main" | grep -E '^ *[0-9]+: +[0-9a-f]+ +< +-:'
```

Each matching row is a branch commit with NO counterpart on main. It clears
E-1803/1864/1865/1929 to zero unmatched, and still flags E-1115, E-1523 and
E-2010 — the branches that really did hold work main lacked. Drop rows whose
commit touches only `.endless/` and what remains is real unlanded work. Cost is
~1.5s on the worst branch here (320 commits against main's 1238), so it is fine
per-task and acceptable for an `--all` sweep.

## Two other readers want this same probe

Keep it one implementation, not three:

- **E-2095 part 2**, the not-on-main report, needs exactly "does this branch hold
  any commit main lacks?".
- **The reaper.** It is gated on `task_landings` — its comment says it "only
  touches dirs whose task has landed at least once" — so a worktree whose branch
  sits at main with nothing to land is settled and disposable but has no landing
  row and is never reclaimed. E-1360 and E-1697 are live examples: E-2084 reset
  both branches to main and both are still on disk holding nothing. The tempting
  shortcut is to record a landing so they reap; that writes a falsehood into the
  exact table the not-on-main report reads. The fix is to let the reaper accept
  "settled with nothing to land" alongside "landed", same TTL, same live-session
  refusal.

## From the description

Switch the probe that unsettled and the session-status marker share to a patch-id comparison.

fields.title: Record sessions paused on a permission prompt
fields.description: Record a session paused on a permission prompt as waiting on the user, using Claude Code's notification hook, instead of letting it read as 'working'.
fields.notes: E-1976 built the display side and left the producer out: its board's first rank has none.
fields.analysis:
## What is missing

Endless installs six Claude Code hooks — PreToolUse, SessionStart,
UserPromptSubmit, PostToolUse, Stop, SessionEnd. None reports that Claude Code is
asking the user for permission, so a session sitting on a prompt reads `working`,
indistinguishable from one doing work. `Notification` is the event that reports
it and was never wired.

E-1976 built the display side and left the producer out: `actWaiting` is the
board's first rank, wears the warning glyph, renders bold, and `classify()`
already routes a state to it. The rank has no producer. That is this task.

## What "waiting on the user" means here

Decided with Mike (2026-09-03): a session is waiting on the user whenever it has
paused for input, whether or not it asked a question. A finished turn and a
question are the same thing for this purpose — the ball is in the user's court —
which is exactly what his tmux window flag already signals and has proven
accurate in practice.

That definition is what keeps the task small. There is no question-versus-
finished classification, no inspection of the turn's final message, and no model
call. `idle` already means "the turn ended", so the work is to add the one
paused-for-input case Endless cannot currently see — a permission prompt — and to
make the vocabulary say that both are the same kind of waiting.

Explicitly not coupled to the minimizer. It is disabled until further notice,
will be renamed when it returns, and nothing on this task's critical path may
depend on it.

## What the current hooks reference says

Checked against the live documentation rather than recall, which was two months
and twenty-four events out of date.

Claude Code exposes 33 hook events. `Notification` carries a `notification_type`
field whose documented values include `permission_prompt` and `idle_prompt`.

Two findings that shaped the design:

- `agent_needs_input` exists but is scoped to agent-team teammates about to go
  idle, alongside a `TeammateIdle` event. It is NOT a main-session "the agent
  asked you something" signal, and designing on it would have been wrong.
- `PermissionRequest` is now a first-class event carrying `tool_name`,
  `tool_input` and `tool_use_id`. It is nevertheless the wrong signal for this
  task: it fires whenever a permission DECISION is needed, which an allowlist or
  another hook can resolve without the user ever seeing anything.
  `Notification` with `permission_prompt` fires when the user is actually
  prompted, which is the fact this task records.

## Why a new state rather than `needs_input`

`needs_input` looks like the obvious home and is not. It is ENFORCED:
`hookcmd.sessionMayWrite` refuses file writes from a session in that state under
`enforce` tracking, with the message "you asked your user something and the
answer has not arrived. There is no command for you to run."

That state means the AGENT asked the USER something. A permission prompt is the
reverse — the agent is trying to act and the harness is asking — and routing one
to the other would refuse the session's next write after the user approved.

The near miss is worth recording because it was not carelessness. The gate's
admission set was a Go `switch` with a silent `default: return false`, so a new
state joined the refused set without anyone deciding it should. That is why
E-2105 came first: with `MayWrite` a named group, a state cannot be added
without the question being answered.

## Why `prompted` may write

Decided with Mike (2026-09-01), from the gate's own stated rule rather than from
preference. The gate admits a session that "has DECLARED what it is working on
and is live-and-acting", and already glosses `idle` as admissible because "a
write from an idle session is by definition mid-turn". A prompt-blocked session
is mid-turn by exactly that reasoning, and the tool it waits on is its own.

The decisive argument was the asymmetry of failure modes. Both readings need a
clearing transition. If the clear misses under this one, a stale glyph sits on
the board until the next Stop — cosmetic, self-correcting. If it missed under the
other, every prompted session would be refused its next write and told there is
no command to run, which is the failure E-2093 was cleaning up after.

## The `needs_input` writers are the real defect underneath

Two writers put `needs_input` in the database and neither means a person is being
waited on: `monitor.InitSession` writes it as a row's initial value at
SessionStart, and the revive-an-ended-row CASE writes it on any incoming hook
(E-1686). Nothing else writes it.

Measured while E-1976 was built: 34 rows in `endless` carrying it, every one last
active 25 to 71 days earlier, none on a pane that still existed — sessions that
registered and never had a turn.

E-1976 responded by excluding the state from the board. Mike's correction
(2026-09-03): that is backwards. Hiding them is how they rotted unseen, the board
already caps each rank at ten rows with a footer naming the remainder — machinery
built for exactly this — and revealing them is what provides the mechanism to
resolve them.

So this task reveals the rows and fixes the writers, and deliberately does not
retire the existing 34. They are surfaced to be dealt with, not migrated away in
the dark. Once drained, `needs_input` has no writer and no rows, and means only
what the declaration gate says it means.

## From the description

Install the hook, add a 'prompted' state to internal/sessionstate classified into all five groups (MayWrite included, so approving a prompt never leaves the session refused), route notification_type permission_prompt to it and idle_prompt to idle, and clear it on the session's next activity.

Waiting on the user means the session paused for input, question or not, so AwaitsHuman becomes the one place that answers it.

Also stops InitSession and the revive CASE from writing needs_input, and reveals those rows on the board instead of hiding them.

fields.title: Export the suite directory to verify.toml checks
fields.description: Export the suite directory to verify.toml checks, as verify.sh suites already get it, so a check can reference its own files without hand-writing the path.
fields.context:
A verify.sh suite gets ENDLESS_VERIFY_RUN/TAP/TASK from the runner; a verify.toml [[check]] gets nothing, so a check needing a file from its own suite directory retypes the path.

.endless/tasks/e-1603/verify.toml does: command = "sh .endless/tasks/E-1603/e2e.sh" — uppercase, where the tracked directory is e-1603. It runs only because APFS is case-insensitive; on any case-sensitive filesystem that check cannot find its own script.

fields.title: Fix idle-session lockout and missing suite path in handoff
fields.description: Fix two gaps: mark an idle session working again when its next turn starts so the write gate stops blocking it, and have the handoff say where a verify suite goes and that it must source the harness.
fields.context:
Two unrelated gaps, folded to hold the backlog.

The PreToolUse gate admits only state='working', so a session that completes one clean turn can never Write again; other states fall into a branch announcing 'No active work session', false for an idle session that holds a task. The refusal names `task claim`, which refuses on status first, and --force clears that only by demoting the task.

Both observed sessions finished through Bash heredocs.

Reporting 'unverified' is not the trigger, only what a session does last.

fields.title: Canonicalize the verify runner's temp HOME
fields.description: Canonicalize the temp HOME the verify runner gives each suite, resolving macOS's symlinked temp root, so suites stop failing for reasons unrelated to their task.
fields.notes: Repointed: the test is not where this belongs.
fields.context:
E-2023's runner hands every suite a temp HOME from os.MkdirTemp, and on macOS the OS temp root sits beneath a symlinked prefix (var -> private/var) — so every suite runs under a HOME reached through a symlink, which a real home directory almost never is.

That is an artifact of the isolation MECHANISM, not a property of the code under test; it is platform-dependent (passes on Linux, fails on macOS); and it makes suites fail for reasons unrelated to their own task, which is the one thing a verification front door must never do.

The whole internal/monitor package then passes under a temp HOME, so the planned per-test fix and the sweep for other HOME-sensitive tests both become unnecessary.
fields.analysis:
Repointed 2026-08-31 by ES-1159 (E-2023), at Mike's direction, after he asked
whether E-2023 could have been implemented so that this task were unnecessary.
It could — and the answer moves the fix from the test to the runner.

## What was originally filed, and why it was the wrong layer

`TestProjectPath_TildeExpandsToHome` (internal/monitor/projects_test.go) builds
its expectation as `filepath.Join(os.UserHomeDir(), "some-project")` and
compares it against `ProjectPath`, which returns the RESOLVED form. The two
agree only when HOME is not itself reached through a symlink. The original plan
was to fix the expectation and sweep for the same shape elsewhere.

The test IS wrong — it compares a resolved value against an unresolved one. But
nothing had ever observed it, and after the change below nothing will again.
Under ED-1550, "noticing something true does not earn a task."

## Where it actually belongs

`makeRunDir` (internal/verifycmd/env.go) takes `os.MkdirTemp("")` verbatim. On
macOS that lands beneath a symlinked prefix, so the runner hands every suite a
HOME reached through a symlink — something a real home directory almost never
is.

Three reasons that is the runner's bug and not the test's:

1. It is an artifact of the isolation MECHANISM, not a property of the system
   under test. The runner's job is to substitute HOME transparently; anything
   else it changes is noise it injected.
2. It is platform-dependent. The same suite, the same code, passes on Linux
   (the temp root is not symlinked there) and fails on macOS. A runner whose
   verdict depends on the OS's mktemp implementation emits false signal.
3. It misattributes failures — this task's own sharpest observation, that "the
   failure it reports will point at the wrong task." That is precisely the harm
   E-2023 exists to prevent.

The counter-argument from E-2023's plan — "a break is a finding, not a
regression" — was written about suites that secretly depended on the real
database, where the dependency was always a contract violation. It does not
transfer. Nothing in the contract says a suite must tolerate a symlinked HOME,
and the runner is not a fuzzer; a deliberate test of symlinked-HOME behaviour is
a thing someone can write on purpose.

## The change

`filepath.EvalSymlinks` on the freshly created temp dir, failing open (a
directory this process just made should always resolve; if it does not, running
under the unresolved path beats refusing to verify).

Measured before and after:

    raw temp HOME       -> FAIL  ProjectPath = "<resolved>" want "<unresolved>"
    resolved temp HOME  -> ok    internal/monitor

The whole `internal/monitor` package passes under a resolved temp HOME, with
that test the only failure under the raw one — so the sweep this task planned
finds nothing left to fix.

## Pinned, not left to the platform

Three tests, because the invariant is invisible on Linux and would rot silently:

- `TestMakeRunDir_IsCanonical` — the run dir equals its EvalSymlinks form.
- `TestIsolatedEnv_HomeIsCanonical` — HOME and XDG_CONFIG_HOME, the values
  consumers actually see, are canonical.
- `TestRun_ScriptSuite_SeesCanonicalHome` — end to end through the real runner:
  a suite observing a non-canonical HOME exits 30 and fails the test.

## Verification of the original symptom, end to end

A throwaway suite driven through `endless-go verify`, whose check was the exact
repro from the original filing, printed a canonical HOME and passed. Before the
change it failed.

## PRODUCT

Nothing macOS-specific in the fix, though the symptom is. Any platform whose
temp root is symlinked hands the same trap to every downstream project's
suites, and the runner is shipped surface.

## From the description

Fix: canonicalize the run dir in makeRunDir with filepath.EvalSymlinks. One line.

fields.title: Surface landed and still-authoritative state for tasks
fields.description: Surface whether a task's work has actually landed and whether a task or decision record is still authoritative, since status is routinely read as answering both and answers neither.
fields.context:
Task status answers "what did we decide about this work".

It is routinely read as "has this code landed?" and "is this record still authoritative?", and it answers neither.

E-2089 measured the cost: E-1115 sat 'assumed' with its fix on an unlanded branch, so the same bug was found and fixed again 14 days later as E-1395; and thirteen tasks read 'confirmed'/'assumed' while the code they describe had been deleted from the base branch, with nothing recorded to say so until E-2089 added the relations by hand.
fields.analysis:
Task status answers "what did we decide about this work". It is routinely read as "is this code on main?" and "is this record still authoritative?", and it answers neither. E-2089 measured the cost: E-1115 sat `assumed` with its fix on an unlanded branch, so the same bug was found and fixed a second time 14 days later as E-1395; and thirteen tasks read `confirmed`/`assumed` while the code they describe had been deleted from main, with nothing recorded to say so until E-2089 added the relations by hand. The same gap has a decisions half — I have repeatedly quoted a task or decision as authoritative without noticing it was obsolete, declined, replaced, or not yet accepted.

Five parts, one problem: the reader cannot see the facts that decide whether to trust the row.

(1) `task show` must STATE landedness for a task in a terminal status rather than imply it by omission. Today the `Landed:` line appears only when a `task_landings` row exists, so "landed before landings were recorded" and "the branch is still sitting there" render identically — as nothing. Three cases, three sentences: `Landed: <ts> <sha>`; `Landed: never — created before landings were recorded (pre 2026-04-22)`; `Landed: never — branch <b> holds N commits not on main`.

(2) Add a "not on main" report — the join nothing does today. Tasks in a terminal status, created on or after the first landing record (2026-04-22), with no landing row OR with a branch holding source commits main lacks. The core is one git call per branch and needs no judgement: `B=$(git merge-base main $BR); git range-diff $B..$BR $B..main`, counting rows whose left side is a commit and right side is `-:`. Drop commits touching only `.endless/`. Use `git range-diff`, NOT `git cherry` — E-2087 asks for a patch-id check, and patch-id is exactly what breaks: `worktree land` rebases, conflict resolution changes the diff, and the branch copy then reads as unlanded forever. Measured on this repo, range-diff clears all four known false-positive branches to zero and still flags E-1115, E-1523 and E-2010; worst case ~1.5s on a 320-commit branch. Mike's framing: this belongs in project status (E-1976), not only in a command run by hand.

(3) Make an excision record what it excises. When a task deletes files another task's landed commits created, emit (or prompt for) the `replaced_by` edge — as E-1449 did by hand for the plan-snapshot deletion and as E-1939, E-2029, E-2074, E-2081, E-1426 and E-1711 did not. `endless task replace <old> --by <new>` already does the right thing once called, including holding shipped work at the status it earned; the gap is that nothing calls it. NOTE: this part needs a recording change first. `task_landings` stores a merge SHA but no base, so the landed commit range cannot be reconstructed, and `task_files` stopped recording 2026-07-11. Persist the landed file set (or the base SHA) at land time and the join becomes exact.

(4) Lead `task show`, `decision show` and their siblings with an IMPORTANT banner when the record is not straightforwardly authoritative: task is obsolete/declined/replaced_by, decision is not yet accepted or has been rejected/superseded. The status line is already on screen and is demonstrably not enough — it is read as provenance, not as a caveat. The banner states the caveat before the content it qualifies.

(5) Say it in the guide, next to (1)'s rendering: a task status answers "what did we decide about this work", never "where is the code".

Scope note: parts 1, 2, 4 and 5 are implementable now. Part 3 is blocked on the recording change named in it; if that makes this task too large, split part 3 out rather than dropping the recording change.

fields.title: Fix Write/Edit block after a bash-input turn start
fields.description: Fix the write gate blocking every Write and Edit for the rest of a turn started with Claude Code's bash input, by marking the session working even though no prompt was submitted.
fields.context:
A turn started with Claude Code's `!` bash-input fires no UserPromptSubmit, so the session is still 'idle' from the previous turn's Stop.

No sanctioned verb recovers it, so the only ways out are to demote the task, send an ordinary prompt, or route around the gate.

Hit live during E-1661 on 2026-08-31.
